. The census counts the U.S. population every ten years.
After the census is taken, a process called

divides up the House's 435 seats among the 50 states. The process begins by giving each state one seat in the House. Then additional seats are assigned so that states with larger populations have more seats than less populous ones. Each state might gain or lose members in the House every ten years, depending on how its population shifts relative to other states.

lessons.name: How a bill becomes a law

pieces.text: In the United States, each law begins as a proposal called a
. Writing and passing laws is the job of the legislative branch. To become a federal law, a bill must move through both chambers of Congress: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

contents.text: The diagram shows the main steps required for a bill to become a law. Read the diagram. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A flowchart showing the steps in how a bill becomes a law. The first step is the bill is introduced in either the House or the Senate.  The chart shows two paths a bill can take. One path shows a bill introduced in the senate and moving through the following stages: Senate committee hearings, Senate debate and vote, House committee hearings, House debate and vote, reconciliation between the House and Senate versions, president's signature or veto.   The other path shows a bill introduced in the House, and moving through the following stages: House committee hearings, House debate and vote, Senate committee hearings, Senate debate and vote, Reconciliation between House and Senate versions, president's signature or veto.

Any differences between the Senate and House versions of the bill are reconciled.
The bill is sent to the House of Representatives, where the committee, debate, and vote process is repeated. The bill passes in the House.

Professional advocates are often employed by organizations to push for legislation that benefits the organization's interests.

contents.text: Read the passage about committees. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: In the House and the Senate, lawmakers are divided into smaller groups called

. Committees examine legislation and conduct investigations into specific areas of government policy, such as education or foreign relations. After a bill is introduced, it is referred to the relevant committee for consideration. Since thousands of bills are introduced in every congressional term, committees help make the legislative process more efficient.
To learn more about a subject, committees hold
. Expert witnesses, lobbyists, and supporters and opponents of the bill are invited to testify at these hearings. Next, the bill enters
. During markup, the committee considers
, or changes, to improve the bill. Finally, the committee votes on whether or not the bill should be sent to the whole chamber for consideration.

textContent.text: Committees have a lot of power over the fate of a bill. Committees can use amendments to change a bill significantly. They can also end the bill's progress by choosing not to hold hearings or voting against sending it to the full chamber for debate. Over 90% of bills "die" in committee this way.

Revise a bill during markup based on public hearings or political priorities.
Hold hearings to learn more about the bill and assess public support for it.
Block a bill from becoming a law by voting against sending it to the whole chamber.

Professional advocates are often employed by organizations to push for legislation that benefits the organization's interests.
State governors or legislators sometimes send
, or written requests, asking Congress to support particular legislation.

After a bill is introduced, it is referred to the relevant committee for consideration. Since thousands of bills are introduced in every congressional term, committees help make the legislative process more efficient.
To learn more about a subject, committees hold
. Expert witnesses, lobbyists, and supporters and opponents of the bill are invited to testify at these hearings. Next, the bill enters
. During markup, the committee considers
, or changes, to improve the bill. Finally, the committee votes on whether or not the bill should be sent to the whole chamber for consideration.

contents.text: Read the passage about committees. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: In the House and the Senate, lawmakers are divided into smaller groups called

. Committees examine legislation and conduct investigations into specific areas of government policy, such as education or foreign relations. After a bill is introduced, it is referred to the relevant committee for consideration. Since thousands of bills are introduced in every congressional term, committees help make the legislative process more efficient.
To learn more about a subject, committees hold
. Expert witnesses, lobbyists, and supporters and opponents of the bill are invited to testify at these hearings. Next, the bill enters
. During markup, the committee considers
, or changes, to improve the bill. Finally, the committee votes on whether or not the bill should be sent to the whole chamber for consideration.

They can also end the bill's progress by choosing not to hold hearings or voting against sending it to the full chamber for debate. Over 90% of bills "die" in committee this way.

contents.text: To ensure leaders do not abuse their power, the Constitution gives Congress the power to remove presidents and other top officials before their terms end using the impeachment process. This process gives the House of Representatives the power to charge an accused official with impeachable offenses which include treason, bribery, and other crimes. Then, the Senate decides whether to convict the accused official. If two-thirds of the Senate votes to convict, the official is removed from office.

questions.text: The secretary of state is accused of bribing a foreign official. The House votes to impeach and three-fourths of the Senate vote to convict.
The vice president is accused of not paying a traffic ticket 15 years ago. The majority in the House vote that this infraction is not an impeachable offense.
The attorney general is accused of destroying sensitive legal documents and impeached by a majority vote in the House of Representatives. The Senate decides not to hold a vote on the conviction.
The secretary of the treasury is accused of stealing money from the government. A majority in the House votes to impeach. The Senate unanimously votes to convict.

pieces.text: The Constitution outlines a detailed process known as the
for electing the president and vice president. Today, the system works like this: First, the people vote in a general election. Then, officials called
from each state meet to cast electoral votes based on their state's general election results. States with large populations have more electoral votes than states with smaller populations.

contents.text: What does the Electoral College do? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It provides an additional step after the general election for representatives of states to officially elect the president.
It gives a recommendation to electors to help determine who becomes president before the general election.
It requires congressional approval for a small group of judicial appointees to choose the president.
It gives states with larger populations more influence than smaller states over who wins the presidency.

contents.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: The judicial branch applies and interprets the laws of the United States.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, gives the judicial branch "judicial power," which is the power to apply and interpret laws. So, the judicial branch applies and interprets the laws of the United States.

content.text: The Constitution establishes a Supreme Court for the United States.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judicial power is "vested in one Supreme Court." Vested in means given to. So, the Constitution establishes a Supreme Court for the United States.

content.text: Congress has the power to set up additional courts within the judicial branch.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judicial power is given to "such inferior courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." So, Congress has the power to set up additional courts within the judicial branch.

contents.text: This choice is not correct:

content.text: The Constitution creates less powerful courts for the U.S. without the input of Congress.

pieces.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judicial power is given to "such inferior courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." Inferior means less powerful. So, additional courts for the U.S. are created
the input of Congress.

pieces.text: Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall described the judicial power to interpret law in the landmark case
. Read an excerpt from Chief Justice Marshall's opinion in the case. Then answer the question below.
It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. Those who apply the rule to particular cases must, of necessity,
and interpret that rule. If two laws conflict with each other, the courts must decide on the
of each.
According to Marshall, what does it mean for the judicial branch to interpret the law? Select

choices.text: The judicial branch tells the legislature which laws to create.
The judicial branch creates new laws to replace older ones.
The judicial branch decides what to do if two laws disagree.
The judicial branch explains what laws mean.

contents.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: The judicial branch decides what to do if two laws disagree.

pieces.text: Marshall says, "If two laws conflict with each other, the courts must decide on the operation
of each." So, the judicial branch decides what to do if two laws disagree.

content.text: The judicial branch explains what laws mean.

explanationText.text: Marshall says that it is the "duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." So, the judicial branch explains what laws mean.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The judicial branch tells the legislature which laws to create.

explanationText.text: Marshall says that the judicial branch can apply and interpret the law, but he does not say that it can tell the legislature which laws to create. Congress, not the judicial branch, decides which laws to create.

content.text: The judicial branch creates new laws to replace older ones.

explanationText.text: Marshall says that the judicial branch can apply and interpret the law, but he does not say that it can create a new law. Congress, not the judicial branch, creates new laws to replace older ones.

pieces.text: Although the three branches of government are separate, each one can
, or limit, the powers of the others. The judicial branch can check other branches through its power to apply and interpret laws in court cases.

contents.text: Match the following court cases to the explanations of how the judicial branch checked the power of other branches.

draggableItems.text: The Supreme Court ruled that restrictions on political ads broke federal law, so parts of the law were overturned. This decision checked the power of the legislative branch.
The Supreme Court struck down the president's order because it conflicted with the will of Congress. This decision checked the power of the executive branch.
A federal district court decided that federal law did not allow the agency to collect this information. This decision checked the power of the executive branch.

contents.text: These choices are correct:

content.text: Congress has the power to set up additional courts within the judicial branch.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judicial power is given to "such inferior courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." So, Congress has the power to set up additional courts within the judicial branch.

content.text: The judicial branch applies and interprets the laws of the United States.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, gives the judicial branch "judicial power," which is the power to apply and interpret laws. So, the judicial branch applies and interprets the laws of the United States.

content.text: The Constitution establishes a Supreme Court for the United States.

contents.text: The judicial branch depends on Congress for some of its power, since the Constitution allows Congress to expand the federal court system. But the Framers wanted independent judges who would not be influenced by Congress or by other factors such as public pressure.
Read part of Article III, Section 1 of the Constitution. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: The judicial power of the United States shall be [given to] one Supreme Court, and such [lower] courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish. The judges, both of the Supreme and [lower] courts, shall hold their offices during good behavior, and shall, at stated times, receive for their services, a [salary], which shall not be [decreased]
during their [time] in office.
Based on the text, in what ways does the Constitution protect judges' independence? Select

choices.text: Members of Congress cannot become federal judges, ensuring separation between the two branches of government.
Article III sets no term limits for federal judges, allowing them to serve for life without needing to be re-appointed.
The judicial branch alone has the power to set up all U.S. federal courts, making it independent of congressional influence.
Judges' salaries can't be decreased, allowing judges to decide cases without fear of having their pay cut if Congress disagrees with their rulings.

content.text: Article III sets no term limits for federal judges, allowing them to serve for life without needing to be re-appointed.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that federal judges "shall hold their offices during good behavior." This means there are no term limits for federal judges, who have lifetime appointments as long as they act appropriately in office. So, federal judges can serve for life without needing to be re-appointed.

content.text: Judges' salaries can't be decreased, allowing judges to decide cases without fear of having their pay cut if Congress disagrees with their rulings.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judges "receive…a [salary], which shall not be [decreased] during their [time] in office." So, federal judges can decide cases without fear of having their pay cut if Congress disagrees with their rulings.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, does not prevent members of Congress from becoming federal judges. The Constitution ensures the separation between the two branches through other means.

content.text: The judicial branch alone has the power to set up all U.S. federal courts, making it independent of congressional influence.

explanationText.text: Article III, Section 1, says that judicial power is given to "such [lower] courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish." This means that Congress, not the judicial branch, has the power to set up lower federal courts.

textContent.text: In 1800, President John Adams wrote a commission, or formal certificate, to make William Marbury a federal judge. The commission was never delivered, and after Adams left office, Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver the commission and make Marbury a judge.

Marbury sued Madison. He brought the case straight to the Supreme Court because Congress had given the Supreme Court the power to directly hear cases involving government officials in the Judiciary Act of 1789. Marbury asked the Court to order Madison to fulfill his duty as a government official by delivering the commission to Marbury.

In its ruling, the Supreme Court argued that its authority came only from the Constitution. The Constitution did not allow Congress to grant the Supreme Court the additional power to directly hear a case involving a government official. So, that section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. Therefore, the Court had no power to order Madison to make Marbury a judge.

textContent.text: In the Deficit Control Act of 1985, Congress gave the comptroller general of the United States the power to cut items from the federal budget, to keep the budget deficit within limits set by Congress. The comptroller general is an officer of the legislative branch and is in charge of monitoring the financial status of the government.

Congressman Michael Synar challenged the Deficit Control Act. He argued that the act essentially asked the comptroller general to enforce a law by deciding which items from the federal budget, passed by Congress, should be cut. Enforcing laws is a power of the executive branch, not the legislative branch.

The Supreme Court agreed with Synar that the Deficit Control Act was unconstitutional. The Court stated the act allowed a member of the legislative branch to have "control over the execution of the laws." This would undermine the separation of powers outlined in the Constitution.

textContent.text: In 1800, President John Adams wrote a commission, or formal certificate, to make William Marbury a federal judge. The commission was never delivered, and after Adams left office, Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver the commission and make Marbury a judge.

Marbury sued Madison. He brought the case straight to the Supreme Court because Congress had given the Supreme Court the power to directly hear cases involving government officials in the Judiciary Act of 1789. Marbury asked the Court to order Madison to fulfill his duty as a government official by delivering the commission to Marbury.

In its ruling, the Supreme Court argued that its authority came only from the Constitution. The Constitution did not allow Congress to grant the Supreme Court the additional power to directly hear a case involving a government official. So, that section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. Therefore, the Court had no power to order Madison to make Marbury a judge.

textContent.text: In 1800, President John Adams wrote a commission, or formal certificate, to make William Marbury a federal judge. The commission was never delivered, and after Adams left office, Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver the commission and make Marbury a judge.

Marbury sued Madison. He brought the case straight to the Supreme Court because Congress had given the Supreme Court the power to directly hear cases involving government officials in the Judiciary Act of 1789. Marbury asked the Court to order Madison to fulfill his duty as a government official by delivering the commission to Marbury.

In its ruling, the Supreme Court argued that its authority came only from the Constitution. The Constitution did not allow Congress to grant the Supreme Court the additional power to directly hear a case involving a government official. So, that section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. Therefore, the Court had no power to order Madison to make Marbury a judge.

textContent.text: In the Deficit Control Act of 1985, Congress gave the comptroller general of the United States the power to cut items from the federal budget, to keep the budget deficit within limits set by Congress. The comptroller general is an officer of the legislative branch and is in charge of monitoring the financial status of the government.

Congressman Michael Synar challenged the Deficit Control Act. He argued that the act essentially asked the comptroller general to enforce a law by deciding which items from the federal budget, passed by Congress, should be cut. Enforcing laws is a power of the executive branch, not the legislative branch.

The Supreme Court agreed with Synar that the Deficit Control Act was unconstitutional. The Court stated the act allowed a member of the legislative branch to have "control over the execution of the laws." This would undermine the separation of powers outlined in the Constitution.

textContent.text: The Line Item Veto Act allowed the president to veto specific taxing or spending provisions in bills passed by Congress, even after signing them into law. In 1997, President Bill Clinton used the line-item veto to cancel sections of two laws. As a result, the City of New York and others negatively affected by the vetoes challenged this act all the way to the Supreme Court.

pieces.text: The Supreme Court ruled in

content.text: Clinton v. City of New York

pieces.text: that the Line Item Veto Act was unconstitutional. Article I requires that a president sign a bill into law or return it to Congress for changes. The Line Item Veto Act violated the Constitution because the president's veto "occurs
the bill becomes law and affects it only in part." Allowing the president to veto only parts of a bill after it has passed effectively allowed the president to change an existing law.

During the Watergate investigation, a special prosecutor appointed by the attorney general issued a

, or court order, requiring President Richard Nixon to hand over a series of tapes he made of conversations with his closest advisors. These tapes were crucial for the investigation into criminal behavior by Nixon's aides.
Nixon refused to honor the subpoena, arguing that a concept called executive privilege gave him the power to withhold information from the other branches of government.

allows the president to keep conversations with advisors private or protect important secrets that relate to national defense or international affairs. Nixon appealed the subpoena to the Supreme Court.
In

, the Supreme Court decided that President Nixon must honor the subpoena and give the tapes to the special prosecutor. The Court agreed that the president has a limited right to executive privilege, but that right is not absolute. Allowing a president to withhold evidence in a criminal trial would interfere with the due process of law.

textContent.text: The Line Item Veto Act allowed the president to veto specific taxing or spending provisions in bills passed by Congress, even after signing them into law. In 1997, President Bill Clinton used the line-item veto to cancel sections of two laws. As a result, the City of New York and others negatively affected by the vetoes challenged this act all the way to the Supreme Court.

the bill becomes law and affects it only in part." Allowing the president to veto only parts of a bill after it has passed effectively allowed the president to change an existing law.
